analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $15 over seven years and ends subminimum wages for tipped, teen, and disabled workers.
analysis.headline: The Raise the Wage Act was introduced with 171 Democratic cosponsors in May 2017, but was never given a vote in the House Education and the Workforce Committee, and the federal minimum wage stayed at $7.25 for the rest of the 115th Congress [S1][S4][S5].
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would raise the federal minimum wage in steps from $7.25 to $15 an hour over seven years, then index it to the growth in the median hourly wage. It would also phase out the separate, lower minimum wages paid to tipped workers, newly hired workers under 20, and workers with disabilities, so all covered workers would eventually be paid the same floor. The bill never left the House committee it was assigned to, so none of this became law in the 115th Congress [S1][S2][S3][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Roughly tens of millions of low-wage workers would gain, especially those earning at or near the minimum wage, tipped workers whose cash wage can be as low as $2.13 an hour, teenagers in their first jobs, and workers with disabilities currently paid less than the minimum under special certificates. Workers would also gain a guaranteed right to keep their own tips [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage in annual steps to $9.25, then $15.00 by the seventh year, and after that automatically increases it with the growth in the median hourly wage of all employees [S3].
Phases out the lower cash wage for tipped employees, raising it by at least $1.15 a year until it reaches the full minimum wage, and guarantees that employees have the right to keep their tips [S3].
Repeals the separate $4.25 minimum wage for newly hired workers under 20, phasing it up until it equals the standard minimum wage [S3].

Ends the practice of paying workers with disabilities subminimum wages: it raises the special minimum in annual steps and sunsets the Labor Department's special certificates after the final increase, while directing the department to help employers transition and keep affected workers employed [S2][S3].
Requires the Labor Department to publish each wage increase in the Federal Register and on its website 60 days before it takes effect, so employers and workers have advance notice [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Businesses that pay at or near the minimum wage, especially restaurants that employ tipped workers and employers that use the subminimum disability certificate, would face higher labor costs. Some of that cost would be passed to consumers through higher prices, and some employers could reduce hours or staffing in response [S3].

drawbacks.text: The increases would raise labor costs sharply for minimum-wage employers. Restaurants that rely on tipped workers face a roughly sevenfold increase in required cash wages, a cost that would fall on small businesses and be passed to customers through higher prices [S3].

The bill sunsets the special certificates that allow paying workers with disabilities below minimum wage, and opponents of that change argue it could reduce employment opportunities for some workers with disabilities; the bill tries to soften this with transition assistance and referrals to competitive employment programs [S2][S3].

A single national minimum wage applies across regions with very different costs of living and wage levels, so the same $15 floor binds more tightly in low-wage rural labor markets than in high-wage cities [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains flow directly to low-wage workers, the group with the least bargaining power in the economy, in the form of a raise that would roughly double the federal floor over seven years. The costs fall on employers of low-wage labor and partly on consumers through prices, and some economists would expect reduced hours or slower hiring at the margin. The bill's phased schedule, indexing after year seven, and transition assistance for disability employers are designed to spread those costs over time. On balance it is a straightforward transfer from low-wage employers and their customers to low-wage workers, with the main honest uncertainty being how much employment adjusts in the lowest-wage markets.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up, so it sat there until the 115th Congress ended in January 2019 without ever coming to a vote [S5].

narrative.text: The Raise the Wage Act was introduced in the House on May 25, 2017 by Rep. Bobby Scott with 171 cosponsors, all Democrats [S1][S3][S4].
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce, which was its only action for the entire two-year Congress [S5].
The committee never held a markup or reported the bill, and the full House never voted on it, so it expired when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].
As a result, the federal minimum wage remained $7.25 an hour, where it had stood since 2009, and tipped, teen, and disabled workers continued to be paid separate subminimum wages [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that pay minimum or subminimum wages are better off because the bill never advanced; their wage costs stayed unchanged, and workers at or near the minimum wage received no federal raise during the 115th Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers paying minimum and subminimum wages

for.name: Rep. Bobby Scott
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Raise the Wage Act and recruited 171 Democratic cosponsors, including the House Democratic leadership (Pelosi, Hoyer, Clyburn).

for.name: 171 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it more than the number of House seats the party held at the time but not a majority of the full chamber.

against.name: Chair, House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee to which the bill was referred never took it up, never reported it, and never let it reach the House floor.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Majority party controlling the House floor calendar in the 115th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a floor vote during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 171 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored it; with Republicans controlling the House, Education and the Workforce committee, and the floor calendar, the bill never got a vote [S4][S5].

industries.note: The industry's tipped-worker subminimum would be phased out, raising the required cash wage toward the full minimum, which directly raises labor costs for restaurants. Those costs come partly at the expense of the tipped workers the industry relies on paying less than the minimum.

industries.industry: Employers using disability subminimum wage certificates
industries.note: The bill raises and then sunsets the special certificates allowing subminimum pay for workers with disabilities, eliminating a labor cost advantage. Affected workers with disabilities are the intended beneficiaries.

industries.industry: Retail, fast food, and other large low-wage employers
industries.note: Any employer paying near $7.25 would face mandated wage increases rising to $15. Higher prices or reduced hours would fall on their customers and workers.
